Emotions During a Change Event
ADAPTING TO CHANGE
The Kubler-Ross Change model was originally developed by Elisabeth Kubler-Ross and 
was based on a 5-stage model of grief; shock/denial, anger, bargaining, depression 
and acceptance. The model has been subsequently modified and extended to address 
the stage of emotion that people experience in their lives or in the workplace during a 
major change event. 
To navigate change effectively, as individuals we need to move through the stages 
quickly to acceptance, and as leaders we need to be aware of the different stages and 
support people throughout the process moving from a current state to a future state 
environment. 
Source; Adapted from Kubler-Ross 1969

Emotional Response to Change – The Key Stages. 
ADAPTING TO CHANGE
Shock 
The cycle begins with a shock, some unexpected news, perhaps an announcement 
at work relating to an organisational change, redundancies, or merger. This can be 
destabilising for the individual and negative thoughts often creep in relating to the 
potential impact it may have on them. 
Denial 
In this stage, emotions often move to thinking that the specific change is not going 
to happen, and ‘won’t affect me’ if it does. It’s not uncommon for people to carry 
on as if nothing has happened, ignoring the potential consequences of the change. 
It’s typical for productivity and performance to decline at this point as people find 
comfort in clinging to the old way of working, losing sight of reality along the way. 
Anger 
As the pending change finally sinks in, emotions often turn to anger or fear. Fear of 
what the change might bring at an individual level, fear of losing one’s job or status, 
or simply fear of the unknown. Anger can surface as people don’t always buy 14 
into the reasons for change. At this point the change initiative has the potential to 
spiral out of control if not addressed and productivity and motivation plummets. 
Bargaining 
Once individuals move out of the ‘anger’ stage they often attempt to delay the 
change or propose an easier and more comfortable alternative for themselves. 
Often this involves trying to negotiate an alternative and find a compromise. 
Depression 
In this stage, individuals lose hope and there are clear signs of negativity, 
sadness, regret and demotivation. This impacts productivity and performance as 
enthusiasm and engagement are at an all-time low. 
Acceptance 
At this point, individuals come to terms with the change and start to think about 
the opportunities that may arise as a result of the change, exploring new ways of 
working in the new model. With any change it’s important to move through the 
stages to ‘acceptance’ as quickly as possible. 
Problem Solving/Integration 
As people start to explore the new opportunities that change may bring, they 
may start to learn new skills and experiment with new ways of working in the new 
environment. Motivation, enthusiasm and productivity continue to rise. In the final 
stage of the change process, the individual has become fully aligned with the new 
way of working and motivation and productivity levels return or exceed previous 
levels prior to the change event. 
The 5 stages as originally defined by Kubler-Ross are summarised below, together with 
additional steps in the change journey where we end up fully integrated in the new 
way of being or working.

Using The Pomodoro Technique to Break 
Your Work into Focused Intervals
Set a timer for 25 minutes and work on a task 
without any distractions. This is one Pomodoro.
When the timer rings take a 5-minute break.
Repeat this process for 4 cycles.
At the end of the 4th period of focus work, take 
a break of 15-30 minutes.
Modify the focus time-period to suit your work 
style - 25 minutes may be too long or too short.
TIP - tracking how many pomodoros a task 
typically takes will aid future time-planning.

The Six Thinking Hats Technique
KEEPING THINGS IN PERSPECTIVE
The Blue Hat: Organisation & Planning/
Big picture perspective – this hat controls 
everything and represents structured thought. 
It is used to decide which hats you’re going to 
put on and the order. And it is used at the end 
to make a decision by pointing out alternatives, 
suggesting new strategies, maintaining control 
and focus, and finally to translate the thinking 
of all the hats into actionable steps.
The White Hat: Information Gathering – this 
perspective is objective and logical. It looks for 
concrete facts by gathering and analysing the 
available information from an objective, neutral 
and unbiased point of view.
The Black Hat: Risk Assessment – consider 
the potential consequences if you act solely 
on your instincts – all the reasons something 
won’t work. This represents the logical-negative 
side including considering the risks, pitfalls, 
consequences, difficulties, and drawbacks, 
drawing on past experiences and shows you 
why certain things might go wrong or not work. 
This will guide you to become more realistic, to 
try new things, and not repeat past mistakes. 
The Green Hat: Creative Thinking, New ideas 
– are you overlooking anything? – encourages 
lateral thinking encompassing originality, 
creativity, crossing boundaries, out-of-the-box 
solutions, making the impossible possible.
The Red Hat: Feelings, Emotions, Instinct and 
gut feeling – encourages you to consider the 
situation in an intuitive, passionate, emotional, 
and subjective way without the need to explain 
or justify. It also helps you understand other’s 
emotions and needs. 
The Yellow Hat: Benefits & Values – what 
opportunities or benefits could arise from the 
proposed course or courses of action? – this 
represents the logical-positive side. Still ruled by 
logic, but by being constructive and optimistic, 
you will explore benefits and opportunities in

Addressing Negative Thoughts
REFRAMING NEGATIVE THOUGHTS | EXERCISE 1
RECORD
Write down what you are saying to 
yourself: E.g. ‘I am not good enough.’ 
‘I won’t get that promotion.’
QUESTION
Ask yourself; ‘What evidence is there to support 
this?’ or, ‘what is another way of looking at this?’ 
Argue with yourself that you are wrong.
ADJUST
Adjust your thoughts so that they better 
reflect the reality of the situation, as 
opposed to your perception of it.
Think of a situation that triggers negative thoughts. 
Then, challenge those thoughts by arguing with yourself:
The first step is to realise you have a choice about how you feel.

How to increase Positivity and Optimism - Best Practice
REFRAMING NEGATIVE THOUGHTS
Avoid negative self-talk – after an event 
consider what you have learned and how 
you might apply that in the future rather 
than focusing on any negative aspects.
Challenge a negative thought – how 
accurate is it? Is it true to say that you 
‘never do anything right’? 
Reframe the situation – look for ways to 
reframe an event in a more positive light. 
Avoid jumping to conclusions: if a 
colleague appears distant or responds 
negatively towards you, rather than 
assuming it is something you did, 
consider what other outside influences 
may be impacting them.
Embrace challenges as opportunities for 
growth “I can’t do this,” becomes “I can’t 
do this yet, but I’m learning.” 
Cultivate a growth mindset. Stimulating 
your brain with new skills/activities/
learning can re-wire your brain, increase 
neural connections, positivity, and 
resilience. 
Positive affirmations: “I can do this” “I’ve 
done this before and succeeded”
Re-direct your attention when re-living 
negative events/outcomes. Listen to 
music, walk, read a book.
Set realistic goals
Take time to savour and bank positive 
experiences into your long-term memory. 
Replay it several times in your memory 
and focus on how it made you feel.
Surround yourself with positive 
influences/people/support network: 
have lunch with positive colleagues 
and get their opinion on any ongoing 
challenges to get a different perspective. 
Practice self-care: take care of your 
physical and mental wellbeing, including 
good nutrition, restorative sleep, and 
regular exercise.
Through the above strategies you can start to reshape your thought patterns and cultivate 
a more positive mindset to create a brain environment that’s more positive and resilient. 
Appreciate the small successes 
throughout the working day. Where 
you are involved in a major project, 
focus on the last few tasks you 
completed to give you a sense of 
achievement. 
Cultivate positive thoughts, for 
example, rather than resenting time 
spent commuting, use it to learn a new 
skill or to review your ongoing tasks.
Make every situation a lesson 
learned: Review tasks or projects on 
completion: consider the challenges, 
what went well, and what you would 
do differently the next time to make 
the next project even more successful.
Use positive language in your 
workplace conversations to create a 
positive environment and make your 
team more optimistic about a project 
or deadline. 
Express gratitude every day 
by reflecting on achievements, 
people, events, such as a successful 
presentation and make sure you thank 
people. 
Find three positive aspects to every 
situation/challenge. For example, even 
though a team project is challenging 
positive aspects may be having the 
opportunity to work with the other 
team members or learn a new skill.
Participate in activities that reduce 
stress and boost mood such as 
socialising with friends, yoga, tai-chi, 
meditation, volunteering, physical 
challenges.
CBT (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy): 
identifies negative thoughts and 
challenges them with evidence.
Mindfulness & Meditation: 
Mindfulness involves being present 
in the moment and observing your 
thoughts without judgement and 
is a good way of breaking negative 
thought cycles.

Use The Pomodoro Technique 
to Focus on Your Priorities 
Set a timer for 25 minutes and work on a task 
without any distractions. This is one Pomodoro.
When the timer rings take a 5-minute break.
Repeat this process for 4 cycles.
At the end of the 4th period of focus work, take 
a break of 15-30 minutes.

style - 25 minutes may be too long or too short.

typically takes will aid future time-planning.

Self-confidence is the belief in our own

Impact of Value Conflict on Organisations
Value conflicts can affect organisational 
outcomes, such as:
‘Value conflict’ - a situation in which an individual’s personal values—such as honesty, fairness, or social responsibility—clash with 
the organisational values or practices, which might prioritize profit, competitiveness, operational efficiency, brand protection etc.
Source: Sullivan, Sullivan, and Bufton 2001
Unethical Practices: When organisations engage in 
behaviours that employees perceive as unethical.
Rigid Policies: When organisational policies prevent 
employees from acting in ways aligned with their values.
Leadership Behaviour: Leaders who model or enforce 
behaviours inconsistent with employees’ values.
Sources of Value Conflict
• Open communication about organisational values and their 
alignment with personal values during recruitment and onboarding.
• Creating opportunities for employees to express concerns and 
suggest changes.
• Cultivating ethical leadership and organisational practices.
• Encouraging value-based alignment in strategic decisions and 
workplace culture.

If you find yourself in the situation where your personal values are 
in conflict with organisational values, consider these strategies:
Best Practice
CLARIFY VALUES
Reflect on which values are non-negotiable for you 
and where compromises might be acceptable.
OPEN COMMUNICATION
Speak with leaders or HR about your concerns in a 
constructive way.
SEEK ALIGNMENT
Look for opportunities within the organization where 
your values align better, such as specific projects or roles.
EVALUATE OPTIONS
If the conflict is untenable, assess whether leaving the 
organization for one with better alignment is the best 
choice for your well-being.
BUILD RESILIENCE
Strengthen your ability to cope with stress through

A HEALTHY AND BALANCED DIET | EXERCISE 2
This exercise takes a more detailed look at your intake of macro and micro-nutrients and 
eating pattern, helping you to assess your current eating habits, the impact this has on your 
mood and energy levels, and highlights areas you can tackle to improve your nutrition and 
well-being:

LOG YOUR CURRENT FOOD INTAKE 
Using one of these Nutrition Apps, log your current 
food intake over 3-4 days, one of which should include 
a weekend day. You should try not to alter your food 
choices or eating pattern at this stage.
At the same time, log your energy levels, mood and 
eating window. 
REVIEW YOUR DIARY –
MAKE ADJUSTMENTS
SET YOURSELF A GOAL 
• Are you eating too much processed food, fats, sugars? 
• Are you snacking into the evening? 
• Perhaps you are missing meals and then over-eating at the next 
meal, or having unhealthy snacks throughout the day? 
• How is your balance of Fats: Carbohydrates: Proteins? 
• Are you getting the right micronutrients and drinking enough water? 
• Can you see a connection between feeling tired or irritable and the 
types of food you are eating?
Having critically evaluated this diary, set yourself a goal, such as to reduce 
unhealthy snacking &/or replace it with healthy snacks, to have regular 
mealtimes, eat more fruit and vegetables, and then make the required 
adjustments to your diet. 
Don’t try to change too much at once, it will increase your chance of 
success if you focus on 1-2 goals. 
With your goal in mind, make adjustments to your diet to make healthier food 
choices at the required daily calorie level, using the APP.
Remember to keep a log of your mood, energy levels and eating window. 
After 3-4 weeks complete another food/mood/energy diary and see the results!
You should also be able to assess your ideal daily calorie intake with the APP. 
If not, then use the one provided by freedieting.com/calorie-calculator.

Improving Sleep Quality - Best Practice
QUALITY OF SLEEP | BEST PRACTICE
Enhance your resilience by incorporating these sleep hygiene habits:
1. Reinforce your circadian rhythm with a regular sleep pattern of 7-9 hours. 
2. Early bird, or night owl? Understand and adapt to your chronotype - do 
focus work when most alert / go to bed when tired, to improve sleep 
quality, energy, mood, performance.
3. Night owls may have trouble sleeping, so try shifting your circadian 
rhythm earlier. Consistently exercising at 7am and good sleep hygiene 
has been shown to shift circadian rhythm.
4. Walk outside within an hour of waking, daylight synchronises your 
circadian rhythm. 
5. Deep Sleep and REM are improved by daily fresh air and exercise. 
They are critical to creativity, memory, learning, insightful thinking, 
and protection against dementia. 
6. Incorporate daily physical activity to improve sleep quality including 
7,000 steps/day preferably outside, evening relaxing exercise e.g. yoga, 
to increase REM, Deep Sleep, and melatonin (primary sleep hormone). 
7. Limit naps to 20 minutes and eat protein at lunchtime to avoid an 
energy slump.
8. Create a bedtime routine to relax your mind and body, such as 
journalling, meditation, reading, breathing exercises or a warm bath. 
9. Good Nutrition helps quality sleep:-
• have your last meal at least 3 hours before going to bed to allow your 
body time to process it.
• avoid alcohol and caffeine sources such as chocolate, tea, coffee, 
and soda from 5pm or earlier. These can cause interrupted sleep and 
reduce deep sleep.
• Increase melatonin production with probiotics such as kefir, eat 
tryptophan-rich foods (turkey, nuts, seeds).
• Choose relaxing exercise not vigorous exercise <60 mins before bed.
10. Make your bedroom as comfortable as possible, at the right temperature 
(c. 65F/18C). Reduce light and sound using black-out curtains, eye mask, 
ear plugs, or white-noise devices.
11. Switch off electronic devices 30-60 mins before bed, they emit blue light 
which inhibits the production of melatonin.
12. If you can’t fall asleep within 30 minutes, get up and leave the bedroom. 
Read or do another quiet activity for 15 to 20 minutes until you get sleepy.

SET YOURSELF A GOAL
This needs to be specific, achievable and something YOU 
want to do. For example, having a brisk 30-minute walk every

PLAN AHEAD
On a weekly basis decide WHEN, WHERE and with WHOM

a friend to join a team sport with you or taking on a challenge 
such as ‘couch to 5k in 9 weeks’.

Invariably something may crop up to potentially disrupt your 
plans – a phone call, your partner is ill, rain, working away

health- say you will ring them back, put on a waterproof, go 
on your own, use the hotel gym. The more you push back on 
the demands of other people, the more they will respect that

When you establish an exercise routine it becomes a habit, 
particularly if it includes daily exercise.

text:
Breathwork and Meditation, including Mindfulness, are known to reduce stress, 
anxiety and depression, and to improve cognitive function including focus, memory, 
and attention span, as well as improved emotional regulation such as mood and 
self-awareness. 
Breathwork is the practice of intentional, 
controlled breathing which offers many physical, 
mental and emotional benefits through its 
influence on our autonomic nervous system. 
These include reduced stress and anxiety, 
enhanced focus and cognitive function 
(creativity, concentration, flow, memory, 
decision-making), improved mood, emotional 
regulation and self-awareness, all of which foster 
greater resilience and wellbeing. The exercises 
below provide an insight into how the power of 
breathing can help you relax, recharge and take 
back control of the way you think and feel.
Ideally when resting, your breath should be 
relaxed, inhaling through the nose, engaging 
the lower torso (and diaphragm) and exhaling 
through the nose. Ideally each breath should be 
‘inhale for 5.5 seconds’, ‘exhale for 5.5 seconds’ 
(coherent breathing).
This provides the optimum flow of oxygen to the 
cells, keeps your system balanced and eliminates 
toxins.
Anxiety and Stress activate the Sympathetic 
nervous system to increase heart rate, BP, 
breathing rate, sweating, as well as increased 
alertness and sensitivity to perceived threats.
Box breathing lowers the activity of the 
Sympathetic nervous system and stimulates the 
Parasympathetic nervous system, resulting in 
reduced physiological arousal, calming the mind 
and lowering stress.
This technique is used by individuals and teams, 
notable Navy SEALS, to stay calm and focused in 
tense situations.
Alternatives
If you find yourself feeling short of oxygen, 
reduce the timings to 3-3-3-3, and increase over 
time.
To relax more deeply to aid sleep vary the 
timings to 4-4-6-2 (Inhale-Hold-Exhale-Hold).
1. Inhale to a count of 4 through 
your nose, using your diaphragm 
and feeling your stomach rise.
2. Hold for a count of 4.
3. Breathe out through your nose 
for a count of 4.
4. Hold your breath for a count of 4.
 
Try to do this for around 4 minutes 
to reach a state of calm and flow.

Jedi breathing /Alternate nostril 
breathing has balanced in and out

use alternate nostrils which forces you

thumb and ring finger to alternately

1. Breathe in and then exhale with a

a count of 8, relaxing your whole body.
 
Repeat 4-10 times.

text:
The diaphragm plays a crucial role in effective 
breathing and oxygen exchange. When you 
inhale it contracts and moves downwards 
creating space for the lungs to help air flow in. 
When you exhale, it relaxes, moves upwards and 
pushes air out of the lungs.
During an in-breath the lower belly expands first, 
followed by your side ribs then the intercostal 
muscles/chest- your belly should move outwards 
before there is any movement in the chest. 
Remember, you are not engaging your stomach 
muscles, they stay relaxed, it’s the downwards 
movement of the diaphragm as the lungs fill 
with air that causes the belly to expand.
1. Sit or Lie on the floor in a comfortable position free from distraction. Relax 
your shoulders. Place one hand on your chest. Place the other hand on 
your abdomen.
2. Trying not to control your breathing, take notice of the rise and fall of your 
hands, the length of each in- and out-breath and how you use your nose 
and mouth to breathe.
3. Then inhale deeply through your nose into your abdomen and laterally 
into the lower rib cage and back toward the spine. Imagine expanding the 
entire surface area and dome of the diaphragm to make room for your 
expanding lungs. Notice how the hand on your abdomen raises higher 
than the hand on your chest. Try not to push out with your stomach 
muscles.
4. Take time to exhale passively through the nose, relax the diaphragm, let 
the stomach return to its starting position.
 
Repeat steps three and four for a duration of five minutes. With practice, you 
should aim to inhale for 5.5 seconds, then exhale 5.5 seconds without a pause 
between the breaths. 
Diaphragmatic Breathwork
Simple Techniques to 
Work on Your Diaphragm

1. Stand Tall: Stand with your feet hip-width apart.
2. Turn your palms towards the floor, elbows facing outwards, middle fingers 
touching, arms straight.
3. Breathe in through your nose, feel your belly rise whilst lifting your hands 
above your head, arms straight, middle fingers touching, palms facing 
away from you.
4. Push your arms towards the sky for 4 seconds whilst holding your breath 
-feel the stretch across your middle and diaphragm, but don’t push from 
the shoulders.
5. Exhale slowly whilst circling your arms round and down by your sides..
 
Repeat 5 times.

Meditation offers significant benefits such as 
stress relief, increased attention span, better 
working memory and knowledge retention, 
better sleep quality, improved mental health, 
enhanced self-esteem, and greater resilience.
Mindfulness, one facet of meditation, reduces 
stress, anxiety, and depression by training 
focus on the present moment, leading to better 
emotional regulation, improved concentration, 
enhanced self-awareness, and better coping 
with difficult thoughts, as well as better sleep 
and potentially lower blood pressure. It enables 
you to observe thoughts without judgement, 
preventing negative cycles and fostering a 
calmer, more positive state of mind.
1. Get comfortable: In a quiet room either lie on your back or sit comfortably on 
a chair or cushion. Close your eyes and focus on your breathing – bring your 
attention to your natural breath -feel the air entering and leaving your nostrils 
or the rise and fall of your abdomen. If your mind drifts acknowledge the 
thought and guide your focus back to your breath.
2. Feet: Start by bringing your attention to your toes, focusing on any sensations.
3. Legs & Hips: Move awareness up to your ankles, calves, knees, and thighs, 
noting tension or heaviness.
4. Torso & Back: Focus on your hips, the rise and fall of your stomach, then your 
back.
5. Arms & Hands: Move to your fingers, hands, wrists, arms, and shoulders.
6. Neck & Head: Bring attention to your neck, throat, jaw, forehead and face, 
softening any tightness.
7. Take a final deep breath, feeling the whole body, and gently open your eyes.  
-If the mind wanders, gently return focus to the body part where you left off.
Benefit
This practice helps reduce stress, improves 
body awareness, and enhances relaxation. Many 
people experience a shift towards calm and 
balance in both body and mind through 
measurable physiological changes, increased 
awareness of the body’s internal state and 
strengthened emotional regulation.
This occurs through:
• Activation of the parasympathetic nervous 
system causing the body to shift from stress 
mode to a relaxed state.
• Lowering of cortisol levels, the main stress 
hormone.

You may experience anger, jealousy, disappointment or resentment. 
These emotions can evoke three types of response:
THOUGHTS
“Why them not me?” “My manager must dislike me &/or 
consider that I am incompetent” “I am being overlooked” 
“Why should I bother in future?” “I’m embarrassed by how 
this may make my colleagues perceive me.”
PHYSICAL FEELINGS
Sweating, tension, rapid breathing.
BEHAVIOURS
Being aggressive towards or avoiding your colleague, 
phoning your partner to have a moan, demanding a 
discussion with your boss.
Recognising these emotional responses can help you to: 
• understand that emotions are responsible.
• prevent emotional thoughts and feelings from turning into actions.
• identify your emotional triggers and negative patterns of thinking 
and behaving.
A colleague is promoted

Managing Emotions
© 2025 S.H.C. Ltd. All rights reserved
Emotions and emotional responses result 
from an interplay between the amygdala 
and the pre-frontal cortex.
The amygdala, part of the limbic system, 
controls automatic lower order brain 
processes characterised by instinct and 
speed, for example, the ‘fight, flight or 
freeze’ response.
The pre-frontal cortex evaluates what is 
happening.
Managing emotions involves strategies to 
delay this response so that the logical part 
of the brain (pre-frontal cortex), can take 
over and respond appropriately.

The Value of Emotions
© 2025 S.H.C. Ltd. All rights reserved
Even negative emotions 
such as the fear of 
exams can motivate us 
to revise. Similarly, regret 
can motivate you to 
learn from mistakes and 
adopt a different course 
of action the next time.
THEY MOTIVATE YOU 
TO TAKE ACTION 
Sadness and despair can 
inspire poetry, music, art, 
and also provoke emotions, 
although conversely, they 
can also paralyse creativity. 
THEY HAVE 
CREATIVE VALUE
Emotions such as shame, 
compassion, love and 
empathy enable us to live 
and work together.
THEY HAVE 
SOCIAL VALUE
They get your attention and 
drive you to take action.
THEY KEEP YOU 
PHYSICALLY SAFE

© 2025 S.H.C. Ltd. All rights reserved
We can use these categories to 
trace a person’s reaction back to 
the primary emotion. This can help 
to explain people’s behaviour, 
motivation and responses.

The primary emotion is anger 
You need to calm down

The primary emotion is fear
You need reassurance

Blocking emotions is stressful and 
exhausting, acting as a barrier to 
developing good relationships.
Staying open to both pleasant and 
unpleasant emotions, and adopting 
flexible thinking, will allow you to 
direct and influence your thoughts, 
feelings and behaviours. 
To successfully manage your emotions you will need to be able to:
Know when to respond 
immediately, and when to 
stop and think.

The Benefits of Managing Emotions in The Workplace
© 2025 S.H.C. Ltd. All rights reserved
By understanding and regulating emotions, individuals can better navigate conflicts, reduce stress, 
and foster a sense of well-being, contributing to a more productive and harmonious workplace.
Enhanced Communication
Managing emotions effectively leads to improved 
communication and empathy, promoting stronger 
understanding and teamwork.
Stronger Relationships
Understanding emotions fosters interpersonal skills, 
including empathy, resulting in more positive and 
productive relationships with colleagues.
Increased Productivity
When individuals manage their emotional responses, 
they are able to maintain concentration and focus, 
leading to higher levels of productivity and efficiency.
Reduced Conflict
Managing emotions allows individuals to respond to 
conflict in a constructive manner, preventing 
escalation and promoting resolution.
Positive Work Environment
A culture where emotions are acknowledged and 
managed constructively fosters a more positive, 
supportive, and engaging atmosphere.
Improved Decision-Making
Understanding their emotional responses helps 
individuals make more considered and rational 
decisions, particularly in high-pressure situations.
Increased Resilience
Being able to manage emotions effectively 
contributes to greater resilience, enabling individuals 
to bounce back from setbacks and challenges.
Greater Job Satisfaction
When individuals feel understood, respected, and 
supported in the workplace this increases job 
satisfaction and sense of belonging.
Leadership Effectiveness
Leaders with the ability to manage their emotions 
effectively are better equipped to inspire, motivate, 
and guide their teams.

Fight or Flight
Early humans were exposed to the constant threat 
of being killed or injured by wild animals or other 
tribes.
The ‘fight or flight’ response evolved to increase 
chances of survival.
It’s an automatic response to danger that allows you 
to react quickly without thinking.
When you feel under threat, the brain automatically 
activates the ‘fight or flight’ response by sending 
signals to release stress hormones that prepare the 
body to fight or run away.
The response is triggered by emotions such as fear, 
anxiety, aggression and anger.
Today, there are fewer physical threats 
but there are more psychological

supportive relationships.

boundaries to maintain healthy and 
sustainable relationships.

Overcoming Imposter Syndrome in the Workplace
IMPOSTER SYNDROME | BEST PRACTICE
• Use Cognitive Restructuring: replace negative thoughts with fact, 
e.g. “I’m not qualified for this job” becomes “I was hired because I 
have the necessary skills and experience”. 
• Keep a journal/Success Bank to reflect upon accomplishments, 
certificates/awards, skills, experiences, successes, milestones and 
positive feedback, including external validation, e.g. recognitions and 
endorsements.
• Self-Assessment: periodically review your strengths and 
weaknesses. Identify areas for improvement and acknowledge 
areas where you excel.
• Professional Development: enhance your skills, capabilities and 
knowledge with workshops, courses, seminars. Keep a skills 
inventory and update regularly.
• Define success: to avoid unnecessary/unsustainable perfectionism, 
define what success means in each role or task and set clear 
achievable goals based on the context.
• Celebrate your Successes: acknowledge compliments positively, 
don’t brush off successes, take time to reflect on a job well done. 
• Cultivate a growth mindset: setbacks and challenges are integral 
to growth and learning.
• Goal setting & Visualisation: set realistic goals, break into achievable 
tasks, acknowledge when completed. Visualise yourself succeeding 
in specific scenarios to boost confidence and reduce fear.
 
Seek Feedback and Mentorship:
• Constructive Feedback/3600 feedback: Regularly seek feedback to 
gain perspective on your performance, support personal/professional 
development and improve self-awareness. 
• Mentorship: Find a mentor, coach or supportive colleagues, who can 
offer guidance, share experiences and provide reassurance.
• Peer Support: connect with others experiencing imposter syndrome 
to normalise feelings. 
• Find confidantes outside your professional sphere to avoid 
comparison if it helps.
